cards.name: Indigo dyeing from Philenoptera cyanescens, West Africa
cards.summary: West African cloth was dyed blue with indigo from the gara plant, a practice used in West Africa at least since the 11th century.
cards.description: The leaves and aerial parts of Philenoptera cyanescens, formerly Lonchocarpus cyanescens, yield an indigo dye. The botanical reference records its use for dyeing cotton and other fibres in West Africa at least since the 11th century. The Tellem cave textiles named in the lead were not confirmed in any source the fetcher could open.
cards.origin_note: The botanical reference gives the use from the 11th century but does not say whether the dyeing was invented locally or arrived from elsewhere.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: the sources describe a widely used West African dye, but they do not measure the scale of its reach.

events.label: by the 11th century CE
events.statement: Indigo from the leaves of Philenoptera cyanescens was used to dye cloth in West Africa at least since the 11th century.
events.quote: yield an indigo dye used in West Africa at least since the 11 th century

open_questions: The Tellem textiles from Bandiagara, dated 11th to 16th century and indigo-dyed according to the Met Museum entries, were not checked: the Met pages returned Page Not Found to the fetcher and HTTP 429 to WebFetch, and the Cambridge chapter opened lists Bolland 1991 but gives no dates for these textiles.
Whether indigo dyeing was invented in West Africa or came with cotton and knowledge across the Sahara is not settled by the sources opened.
The coordinates are an approximate centre for West Africa, not taken from a source.

cards.note: The Science History Institute calls picric acid, made from indigo in 1771, the first synthetic dye, so mauveine is not the first. The 1856 discovery, the 1856 patent and the supply to silk dyers by December 1857 are supported by the Science Museum Group page.
cards.name: Mauveine coal-tar dye, Greenford
cards.summary: William Perkin's mauveine, made from coal-tar aniline in 1856, was patented that year and supplied to silk dyers by December 1857.
cards.description: William Henry Perkin, working on aniline from coal tar, made a black precipitate in the Easter vacation of 1856 whose solution turned silk purple. He was granted a patent on 26 August 1856, and by December 1857 Perkin and Sons supplied the mauve dye to silk dyers from a factory at Greenford Green near Harrow.
cards.origin_note: The sources give the 1856 discovery and patent but do not show that Perkin's work was independent of, or derived from, earlier synthetic colourants.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: the sources show the dye's commercial start, but the wider effect on the chemical industry is not in the pages opened.

events.label: Easter 1856
events.statement: Perkin, experimenting with aniline during the Easter vacation of 1856, found that a solution from a black precipitate turned silk purple.
events.quote: During the Easter vacation of 1856, Perkin was experimenting with aniline

events.label: 26 August 1856
events.statement: The Patent Office granted Perkin a patent for a new colouring matter giving lilac or purple dyes on silk, cotton and wool.
events.quote: On 26 August 1856, the Patent Office granted Perkin a patent for

events.label: by December 1857
events.statement: Perkin and Sons, with a factory at Greenford Green, supplied mauve to silk dyers by December 1857.
events.quote: By December 1857, Perkin and Sons began supplying mauve to silk dyers

open_questions: The source gives a home laboratory for Perkin's work but does not locate it, so England is the broadest place supported; the lead's Shadwell is not in any source opened.
Picric acid (1771) is cited by the Science History Institute as the first synthetic dye. Whether mauveine was the first coal-tar synthetic dye of its kind needs a separate record.
The pace at which German and Swiss firms took the lead is not covered by the sources opened.
The coordinates are approximate centres, not taken from a source.

cards.note: Kizuna gives 1982 as the year Sagawa developed the magnet, and IEEE Spectrum dates the public announcement to November 1983 in Pittsburgh. The sources describe Sumitomo's work as independent of General Motors, so origin is independent; the General Motors work is a separate record.
cards.name: Sintered neodymium-iron-boron magnet, Sumitomo Special Metals
cards.summary: Masato Sagawa developed the neodymium-iron-boron permanent magnet in 1982 at Sumitomo Special Metals in Japan, announced in 1983.
cards.description: Masato Sagawa, after joining Sumitomo Special Metals, developed a magnet of neodymium, iron and boron, which he announced in November 1983 at a conference in Pittsburgh. The magnet is far stronger than the samarium-cobalt magnets of the time and is now used in electric vehicles and wind turbines, among other products.
cards.origin_note: IEEE Spectrum says the Sumitomo and General Motors teams worked without being aware of each other's efforts, so the origin is independent.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: the Kizuna article describes wide applications, but it does not measure the share of people reached.

events.statement: Masato Sagawa succeeded in developing the neodymium magnet in 1982, after joining Sumitomo Special Metals.
events.quote: in 1982, after joining Sumitomo Special Metals (now Hitachi Metals), he succeeded in developing the neodymium magnet.

events.label: November 1983
events.statement: Sagawa announced the neodymium-iron-boron permanent magnet at a conference in Pittsburgh in November 1983.
events.quote: announced the invention of a revolutionary neodymium-iron-boron permanent magnet at a conference in Pittsburgh, in November 1983

sources.title: The Men Who Made the Magnet That Made the Modern World

open_questions: The General Motors melt-spun Nd-Fe-B work by John Croat, announced at the same Pittsburgh conference, is an independent origin of the same compound and should be a separate record.
The EPO page dates Sagawa's move to Sumitomo Metal Industries to 1982, while Kizuna names Sumitomo Special Metals; the company name and the 1982 date need settling.
Osaka, the lead's location, is not named in the sources opened, so the place is recorded at country level.
The coordinates are approximate centres, not taken from a source.

cards.lead: Fibre-tempered pottery in southeastern North America
cards.note: The source gives the Stallings culture as ca. 5150-3200 cal B.P., about 3200 to 1250 BCE, not c. 2500 BCE. It credits Stallings hunter-gatherers with innovating the pottery but does not say whether this was independent.
cards.name: Fibre-tempered pottery, Stallings culture, Georgia and South Carolina
cards.summary: Late Archaic Stallings hunter-gatherers in Georgia and South Carolina made North America's oldest pottery, tempered with plant fibre.
cards.description: The Late Archaic Stallings culture of Georgia and South Carolina innovated the oldest pottery technology in North America, dated ca. 5150-3200 cal B.P. The source gives this as the culture's span, with pottery as its innovation. Whether the technique was invented locally or inspired from elsewhere is not settled by the source opened.
cards.origin_note: The source credits the Stallings communities with the innovation but does not say it was independent of earlier pottery elsewhere, so the lead's claim of independence is not supported.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: the Stallings tradition shaped eastern North American ceramics, but the sources opened do not measure its reach.

events.label: c. 3200 to 1250 BCE
events.statement: The Stallings culture, which innovated the oldest pottery technology in North America, is dated ca. 5150-3200 cal B.P., about 3200 to 1250 BCE.
events.quote: innovated by hunter-gatherers belonging to the Late Archaic Stallings culture (ca. 5150-3200 cal B.P.)

sources.title: Geochemical sourcing of fiber-tempered pottery and the organization of Late Archaic Stallings communities in the American Southeast

open_questions: The c. 2500 BCE date and the claim of independence need a source that gives the Stallings date as an absolute date and addresses the origin question.
Search results mention arguments for a South American or Mesoamerican route for fibre-tempered pottery, but no page making those arguments was opened, so they are not relied on here.
The Mesoamerican pottery case (Purron, Barra, c. 1900 BCE) is not covered by the sources opened.
The 2006 Sassaman, Blessing and Randall article on Stallings Island was opened but its OCR text is too garbled to quote, so it is not cited.

cards.note: EBSCO says Joshua Ward made sulfuric acid as early as 1740 in glass vessels, so the 1746 lead-chamber process is not shown to be the first industrial sulfuric acid. The lead-chamber advance is its larger, cheaper scale.
cards.name: Lead-chamber sulfuric acid, Birmingham and Prestonpans
cards.summary: John Roebuck and Samuel Garbett's lead-chamber process of 1746 made sulfuric acid cheaply in bulk in Britain.
cards.description: John Roebuck and Samuel Garbett produced sulfuric acid in lead-lined chambers at Birmingham from 1746, which were stronger, cheaper and far larger than glass vessels. Because they could not patent the process in England, they moved production to Prestonpans near Edinburgh, from where they began exporting acid around 1750.
cards.origin_note: The sources describe Roebuck and Garbett's process and Joshua Ward's earlier glass-vessel acid, but do not say whether the lead-chamber process was independent of Ward's work.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: the source shows cheaper acid supported the wider chemical trade, but it does not quantify the reach.

events.statement: In 1746 John Roebuck began producing sulfuric acid in lead-lined chambers at Birmingham.
events.quote: In 1746 in Birmingham, England, John Roebuck began producing sulfuric acid in lead-lined chambers

events.label: c. 1750
events.statement: From the Prestonpans works, Roebuck and Garbett began exporting sulfuric acid to the Continent around 1750.
events.quote: they were able to begin exporting sulfuric acid to the Continent around 1750

open_questions: The 1749 date for the Prestonpans works and for Ward's patent need a primary source.
Gay-Lussac and Glover towers and the later contact process need records of their own, with links to the soda and fertiliser records.
The coordinates are approximate centres, not taken from a source.

cards.note: The 2017 Antiquity paper dates the glass-working at Igbo Olokun to between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries AD, which replaces the lead's c. 1000 to 1400 CE. The 2020 paper calls the Ile-Ife technology autonomous, but neither source says it is the only known sub-Saharan primary glass.
cards.name: Glass production, Igbo Olokun, Ile-Ife
cards.summary: Glassworkers at Igbo Olokun in Ile-Ife, Nigeria, made glass beads from local materials between the 11th and 15th centuries.
cards.description: Excavations at Igbo Olokun, within Ile-Ife, recovered glass beads, crucible fragments and glass waste, which the researchers read as local glass production. A 2017 study dates the main glass-working to between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries AD and finds the beads largely independent of glass-making traditions documented farther afield.
cards.origin_note: The 2017 Antiquity paper says the bead manufacture was largely independent of glass-making traditions documented farther afield, and the 2020 paper calls the Ile-Ife technology autonomous.

impact.note: Kept from the lead: the sources describe a regional bead industry, and do not show reach beyond the region.

events.label: 11th to 15th century CE
events.statement: Glass-working at Igbo Olokun is dated, preliminarily, to between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries AD.
events.quote: puts the main timing of glass-working between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries AD

events.statement: A 2020 study reports semi-finished glass in crucible fragments from Ile-Ife as the first evidence of autonomous glass production in sub-Saharan Africa.
events.quote: has provided the first evidence for the existence of autonomous glass production in sub-Saharan Africa

sources.title: Ile-Ife and Igbo Olokun in the history of glass in West Africa
Semi-finished glass from Ile-Ife, Nigeria: implications for the archaeology of glass in sub-Saharan Africa
Evidence of 1,000-Year-Old Glass Production Found in Nigeria

open_questions: The 13,000 beads and the crucible finds come from the 2017 news piece by the excavator, not from a peer-reviewed page; they should be checked against the Antiquity papers.
The 2018 Journal of Archaeological Science paper on the beads could not be fetched; it should be checked for the chemistry and the sourcing.
The lead-barium glass of Warring States China and the mineral-soda glass of South India are candidates for separate records.
The coordinates are approximate centres, not taken from a source.
